tldr: By combining CPGs (central pattern generators) and reinforcement learning in a two-stage framework, a quadruped robot learned 11 diverse gaits and terrain-adaptive styles, demonstrating that every gait can be optimal depending on the combination of terrain, performance metric, and velocity.
hero_caption: Traversing seven challenging terrains—steep slopes, stairs, gaps, rough ground, and step blocks—using 11 distinct gaits (walk, trot, bound, gallop, etc.). Using the same phase couplings, the framework extends to bipedal-mode locomotion standing on front or hind legs and achieves zero-shot validation on real robots (Unitree Go1/Go2).
overview:
Animals switch between diverse gaits—such as walks, trots, and gallops—depending on speed, terrain, and energy demands. Yet in biology and robotics, the question of "which gait is best?" has mostly focused on energy efficiency on flat terrain, leaving open how the answer changes under challenging terrains and different performance criteria (such as base stability or joint smoothness). In quadruped control using deep reinforcement learning (DRL), reward design often causes policies to collapse into local optima where only trotting emerges on flat ground, making systematic comparisons across diverse gaits difficult.

To address this, the authors proposed a hierarchical architecture combining DRL with an abstract oscillator network modeling spinal central pattern generators (CPGs). In Stage 1, while forcibly cycling through all 11 gaits via the CPG coupling matrix, a single policy learns step length, step frequency, and posture styles (base height, foot ground clearance, and foot offsets) for each gait. In Stage 2, with the Stage 1 controller frozen, a lightweight gait-selection policy is trained to optimize user-specified criteria such as cost of transport or base stability.

Large-scale simulation experiments revealed the striking fact that all 11 gaits are optimal (achieve minimal cost) under at least one combination of terrain, performance metric, and velocity. Furthermore, the framework demonstrates remarkable generalization: zero-shot adaptation to an unseen asymmetric gait with three legs in phase, traversing obstacles and gaps far beyond the training distribution, cross-embodiment transfer to a robot five times the training mass, and bipedal-mode locomotion achieved simply by adding a single pitch-tracking reward term.
contributions: Integrated a CPG oscillator network with deep reinforcement learning to acquire 11 classical gaits and terrain-adaptive styles within a single policy across seven challenging terrains.

Decoupled low-level control (Stage 1) from gait selection (Stage 2) in a two-stage training scheme, avoiding convergence to local optima and enabling gait selectors tailored to any user-defined metric (energy savings, stability, etc.) to be retrained in minutes.
Systematically demonstrated for the first time through large-scale quantitative comparisons that all 11 gaits can be optimal under specific combinations of terrain, metric, and velocity.

Demonstrated zero-shot adaptation to unseen irregular gaits, clearances twice the training maximum, cross-embodiment transfer to a quadruped five times heavier, and autonomous locomotion using onboard cameras on real hardware.

sections.heading: Why Do Animals Have Diverse Gaits? A Challenge from Robotics
sections.summary: Re-examining gait optimality not just from flat-terrain energy efficiency, but across diverse terrains and multidimensional criteria like stability and smoothness. A two-stage framework fusing CPG oscillator models and deep RL enables the acquisition and goal-driven selection of 11 gaits.
sections.details:
How quadrupeds smoothly switch gaits depending on speed and terrain has long intrigued researchers. However, biological studies have heavily skewed toward energy efficiency (metabolic cost) on flat terrain, leaving unclear how obstacle avoidance (survival) and stability on rough or stepped ground influence gait choice.

Meanwhile, recent deep reinforcement learning (DRL) for robotics has produced controllers capable of parkour and high-speed running, yet the gaits that naturally emerge often collapse exclusively into flat-ground trotting. Additionally, imitation learning relies heavily on reference data, and model predictive control (MPC) faces prohibitive computational costs when optimizing gait sequences simultaneously.

To overcome these hurdles, the authors drew inspiration from biological spinal CPGs (rhythm generators and pattern formation networks). Constraining 11 gaits based on the Hildebrand classification system via phase relationships of coupled oscillators, a single low-level policy learns diverse terrain-adaptive styles (base height $h$, foot ground clearance $g_c$, sagittal offset $x_{off}$) (Stage 1). Building on this, they proposed a two-stage learning setup where the trained low-level controller is frozen, and a separate, lightweight policy is trained to select and transition between gaits according to specific objectives (Stage 2).

captions.F2: The proposed two-stage control architecture. In Stage 1, foot trajectory parameters are generated based on CPG states (efference copy) and exteroception. In Stage 2, 11 gaits are selected according to the specified objective. On real hardware, a local elevation map is estimated in real time from depth cameras via a compact GRU/MLP.

sections.heading: A Surprising Discovery: Every Gait Has Its Moment to Shine
sections.summary: Exhaustive evaluation across seven harsh terrains and four velocities revealed that all 11 gaits are optimal under certain conditions. The framework also showed exceptional generalization: adapting to unseen gaits, forced parameter changes, a 5x heavier robot, and even bipedal-mode locomotion.
sections.details:
### Testing All Gaits on All Terrains (Stage 1 Evaluation)
Using seven terrains across difficulty levels 1 to 5 (slopes up/down, stairs up/down, gaps, rough ground, and step blocks), 100 robots were evaluated in parallel at four commanded velocities (0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.0 m/s). Three metrics were measured: cost of transport (COT) for energy efficiency, mean base angular velocity for stability, and mean joint acceleration for smoothness.

Remarkably, every single one of the 11 gaits achieved the minimum cost under at least one combination of terrain, metric, and velocity. On flat or easy terrains, energy-saving gaits like the walk and pace excelled. For base stability, the trot dominated in over half of the conditions, but it was best for energy efficiency in only about 25% of cases. Over large gaps and fast stair climbs, dynamic gaits with near fore-aft symmetry—such as the bound and gallop—significantly reduced COT and joint acceleration. Furthermore, an unconstrained baseline without phase coupling (where gaits emerged freely via RL) fell into local optima and failed to outperform the optimal gait in almost all scenarios.

### Optimizing Gait Selection for Specific Objectives (Stage 2 Evaluation)
With the Stage 1 policy frozen, three Stage 2 selectors were trained separately on a parkour course to minimize: (1) power, (2) base angular velocity, and (3) joint acceleration. On flat ground, the power-minimizing policy chose the lateral-sequence walk, the stability policy chose the trot, and the smoothness policy chose the amble. When encountering gaps or large drops, all policies automatically transitioned to bounding gaits to leap across. Each policy vastly outperformed the others on its designated target metric, confirming that task-specific behaviors can be acquired in just minutes of additional training.

### Incredible Generalization and Zero-Shot Transfer
The framework proved remarkably robust even in out-of-distribution (OOD) scenarios:
- **Unseen Gaits**: It adapted zero-shot to traverse stairs at high speed with an artificial limping coupling—where three legs are in phase and the remaining leg is in antiphase—a pattern never seen during training.
- **Style Overrides**: Forcing foot clearance to twice the training maximum (0.24 m) or clamping base height to its minimum did not cause the robot to fall, successfully leaping over gaps.
- **Extreme Unseen Terrains**: The robot galloped over 0.8 m gaps (roughly 50% wider than the training maximum of 0.55 m) and scaled 0.4 m stairs (60% higher than during training).
- **Cross-Embodiment Transfer**: A single controller trained on the compact Unitree Go1 transferred zero-shot without retraining to the Go2, the Aliengo (2x mass), and the B2 (5x mass, 2.15x height). Operating in CPG oscillator space rather than joint torque space made this possible.

### Extension to Bipedal-Mode Locomotion
By adding just a single pitch-tracking reward term to Stage 1, bipedal-mode locomotion was achieved standing on either the front legs (handstand walking) or the hind legs. Without additional demonstrations or curriculum learning, the robot traversed stairs and skipped obstacles while maintaining all 11 leg phase couplings.

captions.F3: Distribution maps of the optimal gaits minimizing COT (cost of transport), base angular velocity, and joint acceleration across seven terrains, difficulty levels 1-5, and four commanded velocities. All 11 color-coded gaits claim cells on the grid, proving that no universally superior gait exists.
captions.F4: Stage 2 gait selection experiments on a parkour course with consecutive diverse terrains. (a) Course overview, (b) selected gaits and adapted posture style parameters for the power-minimization policy, (c) gait usage breakdown for each objective-driven policy, and (d) graphs showing that each policy successfully minimized its target metric.
captions.F5: Generalization tests under out-of-distribution conditions. (a) Unseen irregular gait with three legs in phase, (b, c) stair climbing with foot clearance forced to twice the training maximum, (d-f) gap leaps under extreme posture settings, and (g-i) zero-shot transfer to larger quadrupeds with up to 5x higher mass (Go2, Aliengo, B2).
captions.F6: Bipedal-mode locomotion acquired by adding a single pitch-tracking reward term. Both front-leg handstand (top) and hind-leg walking (bottom) negotiate rough terrain and stairs while preserving all 11 leg phase couplings.

sections.heading: Takeaway: Why Relying on a Single Gait Is a Trap
sections.summary: The finding that every gait is optimal somewhere strongly supports the hypothesis that animal gait diversity evolved for survival and multi-objective adaptability. Furthermore, combining a two-stage design with strongly coupled CPGs proves crucial for escaping local optima in robotic exploration.
sections.details:
The central takeaway of this work is that every gait has an inherent reason to exist. Intuitively, high-energy, seemingly awkward gaits like the pronk (all four legs bouncing simultaneously) might seem evolutionary dead ends. Yet on stairs with specific cadences, the pronk emerged as the optimal strategy to maximize base stability. Conversely, the trot—which emerges most readily in standard reinforcement learning—was optimal for energy efficiency in only 25% of conditions, underscoring how conventional end-to-end single-gait training gets trapped in local optima.

Decoupling low-level control from gait selection in two stages plays a vital role. Forcibly sampling gaits across all terrains during low-level training guarantees the acquisition of an exhaustive gait repertoire. Training gait selection concurrently would cause the policy to collapse prematurely into a single initially stable gait (such as trotting), abandoning exploration of other strategies. Once Stage 1 is frozen, the Stage 2 selector can be retrained for any new objective in minutes.

The oscillator coupling weight $w_{ij}$ is equally critical. Weak coupling allows the policy to distort phases arbitrarily; strong coupling ($w_{ij}=10$) was essential to enforce specified gaits. In nature, fruit flies exhibit weak inter-leg coupling at low speeds and switch to strong coupling at high speeds. Dynamically adjusting coupling strength based on velocity represents an exciting direction for future research.

A limitation is that the current controller is primarily optimized for motion within the sagittal plane (fore-aft and vertical). As a result, it struggles to recover from rollovers when encountering asymmetric step blocks at an angle. Incorporating lateral foot placement control remains an important next step.

sections.heading: Under the Hood: CPG Formulations and Two-Stage RL Implementation
sections.summary: A deep dive into the technical details: the Hopf-based CPG rhythm generator, the pattern formation layer mapping footsteps into Cartesian space, input/output and reward designs for Stages 1 and 2, and elevation map distillation via DAgger for real-world deployment.
sections.details:
### Rhythm Generation and Pattern Formation (CPG Model)
The oscillator assigned to each leg $i$ is modeled via amplitude $r_i$ and phase $\theta_i$ dynamics. Using target amplitude $\mu_i$, intrinsic angular frequency $\omega_i$, convergence rate $a$, coupling weight $w_{ij}$, and phase bias $\phi_{ij}$, inter-leg phase differences are enforced through the coupling term $\sum_j w_{ij} \sin(\theta_j - \theta_i - \phi_{ij})$. A strong coupling weight ($w_{ij}=10$) is used, and a $4\times 4$ phase difference matrix $\bm{\Phi}$ corresponding to one of the 11 gaits is selected.

The pattern formation layer maps oscillator outputs into target Cartesian foot positions. Foot trajectories follow geometric ellipses defined along the fore-aft axis by step length $d_{step}$ and offset $x_{off}$, and along the vertical axis by base height $h$, maximum swing clearance $g_c$, and stance ground penetration $g_p$. Target positions are tracked via inverse kinematics (IK) and a 1 kHz PD controller.

### Stage 1: Unified Training Across All Gaits and Terrains
Using Isaac Gym, 4,096 Unitree Go1 robots are simulated in parallel and controlled via PPO at 33 Hz. The state space comprises commanded velocity, an elevation map ($17\times 11$ grid), angular velocity, base orientation, joint angles/velocities, previous actions, and the noiseless internal CPG states ($\bm{r}, \bm{\theta}, \dot{\bm{r}}, \dot{\bm{\theta}}$)—analogous to biological efference copies—alongside the gait index. The action space is $\bm{a}_{t,s} = [h, g_c, x_{off}, \bm{\mu}, \bm{\omega}] \in \mathbb{R}^{11}$. Rewards only penalize velocity tracking error, unwanted base oscillations, and abrupt joint movements; no rewards enforce posture styles.

### Stage 2: Task-Specific Gait Selector
The trained Stage 1 network is frozen. An MLP takes the same observations and outputs an 11-dimensional gait-selection vector $\bm{a}_{t,g}$. The gait chosen via argmax dictates the phase difference matrix $\bm{\Phi}$. Trained with an action-rate penalty to prevent excessive gait switching alongside objective-specific rewards (low power, reduced angular velocity, etc.), training converges in minutes.

### Onboard Elevation Map Estimator (Sim-to-Real)
For real-world transfer, a network was built to regress elevation maps from a front-facing RealSense D435i depth camera ($48\times 16$) and proprioception. Combining a CNN with a GRU (256 hidden units), it integrates past observations to retain blind-spot terrain information beneath the robot. Distilled on the policy's own rollouts using DAgger, this prevents the accumulation of prediction errors during physical deployment.

sections.heading: Appendix: Phase Definitions of 11 Gaits and Tracking Accuracy
sections.summary: Summarizing the phase offset definitions based on the Hildebrand classification for the 11 gaits and the artificial test gait, confirming high phase-tracking fidelity in real deployment.
sections.details:
The 11 gaits based on the Hildebrand classification are defined by phase differences $\phi_{ij} \in [0, 2\pi)$ corresponding to touchdown timings within a gait cycle across legs (front-right FR, front-left FL, hind-right HR, hind-left HL).

- **Symmetrical Gaits**: Trot (diagonal pairs synchronized with a $\pi$ phase offset), pace (ipsilateral pairs synchronized with a $\pi$ offset), pronk (all four legs synchronized), and various walks (lateral-sequence, diagonal-sequence, etc., where each leg touches down with a 25% phase shift).
- **Asymmetrical and Leaping Gaits**: Bound (fore and hind pairs alternately synchronized), half-bound, canter, transverse gallop, and rotary gallop.
- **Artificial Test Gait**: An unnatural gait where three legs are fully in phase (phase 0) and the remaining leg is in antiphase (phase $\pi$).

These gaits are formulated into a $4\times 4$ phase difference matrix $\bm{\Phi}$ and fed into the oscillator dynamics. In simulation evaluations, robots achieved 95% to 100% ground contact during commanded stance phases, demonstrating exceptionally high gait-tracking accuracy (except during brief airborne moments when leaping wide gaps where no ground support physically exists).

captions.F7: Touchdown timings for each leg across a gait cycle for the 11 evaluated gaits and the artificial test gait (three legs in phase). Relative phase lags between fore, hind, left, and right legs are defined as percentages and converted into the CPG coupling matrix.

takeaways: There is no single "best" gait; across challenging terrains, every one of the 11 gaits finds an optimal niche depending on whether energy efficiency, stability, or smoothness is prioritized.

Decoupling low-level execution (tracking gaits and styles) from high-level selection (deciding gaits) prevents reinforcement learning from falling into local optima, enabling task-specific adaptation in minutes.

Framing the action space around CPG oscillator parameters rather than joint torques enables remarkable zero-shot transfer to quadrupeds five times heavier and seamless adaptation to unseen, unnatural gaits.
limitations: The current controller focuses primarily on sagittal plane (fore-aft and vertical) motions and lacks independent lateral foot placement, limiting its ability to recover from rollovers when negotiating asymmetric obstacles diagonally.
Stage 2 optimization only selects and transitions between gaits; it does not directly fine-tune the frozen Stage 1 foot trajectory parameters or posture styles for new performance criteria.
Simulation environments were restricted to rigid terrains, leaving open how well these gaits perform and adapt across deformable or fluid substrates like mud, snow, water, and sand.
